preamble: Unrounding of the close-mid front rounded vowel [ø(ː)] to [e(ː)], merging it with the plain front vowel. In Old English, /ø(ː)/ from the i-umlaut of o and ō was unrounded to /e(ː)/ in Kentish by the late 9th to early 10th century: Kentish charters still mostly write oe but already have gerefa 'reeve' beside geroefa, and the Kentish Glosses write efst for Old English oefstan 'to hasten'. West Saxon unrounded the vowel in the 9th–10th centuries, and the merger was complete in Late West Saxon.

examples.note: Wiktionary lists grœ̄ne as the Anglian and early Kentish form of grēne.
The Kentish Glosses already write efst for oefstan (Steponavičius 1978).
The Germanic umlaut article traces *fōti > *fø̄ti > fø̄t > fēt. Old English phonology places the unrounding in West Saxon and Kentish by about 900; Anglian long /øː/ generally stayed rounded.

sources: Steponavičius, A. (1978). The development of front rounded monophthongs in Old and Middle English dialects. Kalbotyra, 29(3), 56-67. https://www.journals.vu.lt/kalbotyra/article/view/21866
